newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian budget seen disappointing foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: Indian budget seen disappointing foreign investors.

text.p: India's federal budget to be unveiled next week will disappoint foreign investors with half-measures set by the country's cash-strapped ruling coalition, analysts said on Tuesday.
"Don't expect too much from the budget," cautioned Sanjeev Mohta, head of research at securities firm James Capel B&K.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram -- due to present the 1997/98 (April-March) budget on February 28 -- is unlikely to announce key cuts in corporate taxes, analysts said.

They said the United Front government led by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda needed to worry about a chronic fiscal deficit that is unlikely to be capped at the targeted five percent of gross domestic product in 1996/97.
The nation's fiscal deficit hit 5.9 percent of GDP in 1995/96 and 6.1 percent in 1994/95.

The deficit is projected to reach 682.66 billion rupees ($19.02 billion) in 1996/97 against the budgeted figure of 622.66 billion ($17.36 billion), and against 640 billion ($17.83 billion) in 1995/96, according to the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy, and independent Bombay-based think tank.
"This year the finances have been hit by a double whammy on both the fronts, lower receipts and higher expenditure," ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec) said in a report.

"The higher fiscal deficit and absence of any substantial measures to boost corporate growth should keep the sentiments down in equity markets," it warned, advising investors to sell in the event of a pre-budget stocks rally.
I-Sec is an affiliate of U.S. investment bank J.P. Morgan.

Analyst Girish Kumar of Merrill Lynch & Co in Singapore said Chidambaram could announce capital market reforms. He cited the scrapping of a dividend tax for firms in core sectors like power and telecommunications, and the relaxation of limits on shares held by foreign investors.
Currently foreign institutional investors can hold equity of up to 24 percent in a company and up to 20 percent in the State Bank of India, which is governed by a separate act.
"But these are still parts of the whole. He has to do something drastic about the fiscal deficit and we don't see any new initiatives there," Kumar said.
Capel B&K's Mohta urged Chidambaram to address investor confidence which he said has been eroded by political infighting and the lack of clear policies for infrastructure projects.

India is believed to have attracted just over $2 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI) in 1996. The government has set a goal of $10 billion over several years but analysts say a rash of litigation and delays in approvals have made investors wary.
Official figures show FDI inflows were at 63.1 billion rupees ($1.76 billion) between January and October 1996 against 63.7 billion ($1.77 billion) in calendar 1995.
Foreign portfolio investment inflows have dropped to $119.6 million between January 1 and February 12, 1997, compared with $706.7 million in the first two months of calendar 1996.
"Ultimately, he (Chidambaram) has to improve the investment scenario. How he plans to do that is the real question," Capel's Mohta said.
"The government is too busy fighting over small things. It will be difficult for them to come to a consensus," he added.
Analysts said squabbles within the 13-party coalition were likely to result in a compromise budget.
"What you have to watch out for is that each different ministry will have their own agenda," said Anand Aithal, a strategist at Goldman Sachs in Hong Kong.
He cited an airline project between India's Tata group and Singapore Airlines which was recently approved by the Foreign Investment Promotion Board but opposed by the Civil Aviation Ministry.
"Bits of reforms will happen but we just have to get used to compromise and half measures as long as we have a coalition government," said Aithal. ($1 = 35.89 rupees)
